A mud-brick mosque in Bobo-Dioulasso, in western Burkina Faso, built in the 1880s in the Sudano-Sahelian style, with conical towers and wooden beams sticking out of its walls.

It was built by the Dioula, Muslim traders of Mande origin who settled among the Bobo farmers, and the town's name joins the two peoples. Like the Great Mosque of Djenne, its walls must be replastered with mud often. Bobo-Dioulasso became a junction of the railway from Abidjan in 1934 and is the country's second city and a centre of music. See also Islam in West Africa.
